sections.h2: What are the ways to sell a house quickly in Cary?
sections.html:
Cary owners who want speed usually choose between a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is and a traditional listing that takes longer but exposes the home to more buyers. The right choice depends on the condition of the house, the loan balance, and how soon you need the money.

A listing asks you to prepare the home, allow showings, and wait through a buyer's inspection and financing. A direct cash sale skips most of that, and the buyer usually takes the home with its repairs. What both routes share is a recorded deed at the register of deeds, so the paperwork steps below apply either way.

  • Check your payoff with your lender before you compare any offer.
  • Ask each buyer which costs they expect you to cover at closing.
  • Find out which county records your parcel, because Cary spans more than one.
  • Confirm whether any special assessment or deferred tax sits on the property.

sections.h2: How did Cary grow, and why does that matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Cary grew from a railroad-era village into one of the largest towns in the Triangle, and most of its housing was built during the last few decades. The town traces its roots to a 1750s settlement called Bradford's Ordinary, and its official history credits Allison Francis Page, who bought 300 acres in 1854, as its founder. Cary was incorporated in 1871, according to the Town of Cary history page.

The same page says Research Triangle Park, developed in the 1960s, turned a quiet town of a few thousand people into a booming bedroom community. The population nearly tripled in the 1970s to 21,763, then doubled in the 1980s and again in the 1990s. The town now describes itself as a community of over 191,000 people from more than 60 nationalities.

For a seller, that history explains the housing stock. Much of Cary's residential stock dates from the growth decades, so buyers often compare your house against subdivisions with similar layouts, and updates such as kitchens, roofs and mechanical systems weigh heavily in how they price it.

sections.h2: Which county taxes a house in Cary?
sections.html:
It depends on where the parcel sits, because Cary's limits now span Wake, Chatham and Durham counties. The town's taxes and assessments page says each county handles assessment, valuation, billing and collection for the Town of Cary, so Cary itself does not bill you.

Most Cary homes are in Wake County. Wake's tax office bills and collects for towns inside the county, and its 2026 tax bill page says the commissioners voted on June 1 to adopt a budget with a county rate of 53.71 cents. That page also notes that people paying through mortgage escrow are not mailed a bill, so check the online portal when you sell.

The table lists the three offices the town points owners to, with the phone numbers the town prints for each.

The Cary town rate changes with each budget. Ask the county tax office for the rate on your parcel rather than relying on an older figure.

sections.h2: What happens to the property tax bill when a Cary house sells?
sections.html:
The tax bill stays attached to the property until it is paid, so it gets settled at or before closing. North Carolina bills taxes for a fiscal year, and they fall due on September 1, but they are payable without interest until the first week of January. Wake's page puts the no-interest deadline at January 5.

Wake County also offers short-term payment plans and accepts partial payments in any amount as long as the balance is clear by that date. Its page warns that after the bill becomes overdue, Tax Administration cannot help, and past-due taxes can be taken from paychecks, bank accounts or rent.

  • Ask the title company to confirm the current year's bill is paid or prorated.
  • Check for a vehicle or special fee that rode on the same bill.
  • If an escrow account paid the tax, expect a refund of leftover escrow from the lender.

sections.h2: Do tax relief programs affect a sale in Cary?
sections.html:
Yes, if the owner receives one of North Carolina's three relief programs, because a sale can end the benefit and trigger deferred taxes. Wake's page lists a senior and disabled program, tax deferment, and a disabled veteran program, with a June 1 filing deadline set by state law and late applications considered for good cause.

The state statute for the elderly or disabled exclusion removes the greater of $25,000 or fifty percent of appraised value from taxation for eligible owners at least 65 or disabled, and the disabled veteran exclusion removes the first $45,000 of appraised value, with no age or income limit. The circuit breaker is different: it limits taxes to a share of income and defers the rest as a lien, and under G.S. 105-277.1B a transfer of the property makes the deferred taxes for the preceding three fiscal years due.

If you or a parent receives any of these benefits, ask the county tax office what will come due before you accept an offer. A buyer will not take on that balance.

sections.h2: What does the state charge to record a deed in Cary?
sections.html:
The seller pays the state's excise tax and the recording fee is small by comparison. Under G.S. 105-228.30, the tax is one dollar on each five hundred dollars of consideration or fraction of it, and the transferor pays it to the register of deeds before the deed is recorded.

Recording fees are set statewide in G.S. 161-10: a general instrument costs $26.00 for the first 15 pages plus $4.00 for each extra page, a deed of trust costs $64.00 for the first 35 pages plus $4.00 for each additional page, and recording a satisfaction of a deed of trust carries no fee. Under G.S. 47-18, a conveyance only protects the buyer against lien creditors and later purchasers from the time it is registered, so recording promptly matters.

Because Cary parcels fall in three counties, the register of deeds you use is the one for the county where the land lies. Your closing attorney will confirm which.

sections.h2: What if the Cary house is in foreclosure or part of an estate?
sections.html:
Both situations have fixed state timelines, and both are better handled early. A North Carolina foreclosure is heard by the clerk of superior court, with notice of hearing served at least 10 days ahead under G.S. 45-21.16. After a sale, anyone can raise the price through an upset bid within ten days, which must top the earlier bid by at least 5 percent and not less than $750, per G.S. 45-21.27.

Selling before the foreclosure sale can keep that process from running. For inherited property, a small estate may be handled by affidavit under G.S. 28A-25-1 when personal property after liens does not exceed $20,000, but a house usually calls for the clerk's office in the county where the decedent lived. North Carolina repealed its estate tax for deaths on or after January 1, 2013.

faqs.q: Is the Town of Cary the one that bills my property tax?
faqs.a: No. The town says each of Wake, Chatham and Durham counties assesses, bills and collects the tax for Cary, so you pay the county that covers your parcel. The town's municipal rate is added to your county bill.

faqs.q: By what date must Cary homeowners pay the tax bill without interest?
faqs.a: January 5. Wake County's page says taxes are due September 1 and must be paid by January 5, 2027 for the 2026 bill to avoid interest. State law starts interest in January once that period ends.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed excise tax when a Cary home sells?
faqs.a: The seller, who is the transferor. North Carolina sets it at $1.00 per $500 of value or fraction, paid to the register of deeds before the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Does recording a satisfaction of my mortgage cost anything?
faqs.a: No. The statewide fee schedule lists no charge for recording the satisfaction or cancellation of a deed of trust or mortgage.

faqs.q: Can a Cary senior keep a tax break after selling?
faqs.a: No benefit follows the owner to a new property automatically. Each exclusion needs a new application with the county, and the circuit breaker's deferred taxes come due when the property is transferred.
